newsitem.title: USA: Music labels have hit-and-miss quarter.
newsitem.headline: Music labels have hit-and-miss quarter.

text.p: Music helped soothe the box office disappointments of some of the world's major entertainment companies in the first quarter, but uneven album sales and continued pricing pressures hurt other record labels.

"My sense is there's some improvement in the U.S. record industry, but it was centred on a few hit albums and it's still not clear if the first quarter's momentum will continue through the year," Sanford Bernstein analyst John Penney said Friday.
Analysts expect lackluster sales and weak pricing to cause U.S. record industry-wide operating income to fall by 10 percent in 1997 after falling more than 20 percent in 1996.

"The only way the record industry can meaningfully accelerate operating income growth is through vigorous attention to cutting overhead and maintaining tight cost control in developed markets," Penney said.
Worldwide recorded music sales rose 5.5 percent to $39.8 billion in 1996 -- a far cry from double-digit growth in the early 1990s. U.S. unit shipments and revenues rose only 2 percent.

Despite the record industry's woes, music still proved to be the more dynamic show business arm at some of the biggest entertainment giants where the more glamorous movie units suffered from high costs and box office disappointments.
The world's six big labels include Time Warner Inc.'s Warner Music, Sony Corp., Seagram Co. Ltd.'s Universal Music Group, Polygram NV, Bertelsmann AG's BMG and EMI Group Plc.

For instance, weak film performance was offset by improved music results during the first quarter at Dutch-based Polygram, where reductions in overhead and restructuring at its Motown label contributed to the bottom line.
Polygram Music's sales grew by 9 percent and operating income rose by 19 percent, boosted by hit albums such as U2's "POP," which sold nearly 5 million units worldwide.

A turnaround at Universal Music Group overcame a downturn at its film studio and helped Universal's parent, Seagram, double its net profit in the March quarter to $27 million on 8 percent higher revenues of $2.8 bilion. Universal Music revenues soared 61 percent to $367 million.
Universal's results were boosted by its aggressive expansion mode and its 50 percent ownership of the hot Interscope label, which has many hit acts like "No Doubt" on its roster.
U.S. recording industry market leader Time Warner Inc.'s first quarter earning figures, however, showed continued weakness in its music divisions.
Warner Music Group posted first quarter earnings before interest, taxes and other items of $140 million vs. $146 million for the same period in the prior year.
Music revenues dropped to $933 million from $983 million but the company held a lead in the U.S. market share with 21 percent in the quarter.
"The industry's still going through a recovery mode but it's going to probably take a few quarters before we get the numbers working, said Chris Dixon, of Painewebber.
Analysts said the labels must concentrate on cost control, particularly amid rising marketing and promotion and talent costs in the face of slower top line growth.
On Thursday, Sony reported its music unit's global full year sales climbed 14 percent to $4.72 billion, driven by some hit albums.

"Sales in the music group continued to rise despite the weak retail environment in the United States, primarily due to favourable sales growth outside Japan," a Sony spokesman said referring to the full year and quarter.
One notable success was Canadian pop diva Celine Dion's album "Falling Into You," which won two Grammys and has sold more than 21 million copies since its March 1996 release.
Sony Music Entertainment Japan, its Japan music subsidiary, however, said its earnings in the year to March 31 fell sharply due to a shortage of big hits.
The U.S. market is experiencing a painful maturation process and European markets also remain weak, except for Britiain, analysts said.
"Latin America and parts of Asia are proving the bright spots for the industry," said Penney.

All the record labels operate globally but the largest international companies are Polygram, EMI, Sony and Bertlesmann. Warner and Universal drive a greater proportion of their revenues from the U.S. market than the others, analysts said.
